questions.problem: The remainder of dividing $2{x}^{4}+{x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}-3x-7$ by $x+1$ is{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Let $p(x)=2{x}^{4}+{x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}-3x-7.$ 

The remainder theorem states that when $p(x)$ is divided by $(x+1),$ the remainder equals $p(-1).$ 

Evaluating $p(-1)$ directly gives

$$
\begin{aligned}p(-1) & =2(-1)^{4}+(-1)^{3}-2(-1)^{2}-3(-1)-7 \\  & =2-1-2+3-7 \\  & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$

So, when $p(x)$ is divided by $(x+1),$ the remainder is $-5.$

**Note:** We can check the answer by carrying out synthetic division:

|  | ${x}^{4}$ | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $-1$ | $2$ | $1$ | $-2$ | $-3$ | $-7$ |
|  | $↓$ | $-2$ | $1$ | $1$ | $2$ |
|  | $2$ | $-1$ | $-1$ | $-2$ | $-5$ |

questions.problem: Find the remainder of the division $\frac{-3{x}^{4}+7{x}^{3}-4{x}^{2}-x+7}{x-2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $p(x)=-3{x}^{4}+7{x}^{3}-4{x}^{2}-x+7.$ 

The remainder theorem states that when $p(x)$ is divided by $(x-2),$ the remainder equals $p(2).$ 

Evaluating $p(2)$ directly gives

$$
\begin{aligned}p(2) & =-3(2)^{4}+7(2)^{3}-4(2)^{2}-2+7 \\  & =-48+56-16-2+7 \\  & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

So, when $p(x)$ is divided by $(x-2),$ the remainder is $-3.$

**Note:** We can check the answer by carrying out synthetic division:

|  | ${x}^{4}$ | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $2$ | $-3$ | $7$ | $-4$ | $-1$ | $7$ |

questions.problem: Find the value of $k$ if the remainder of the division $\frac{{x}^{3}+kx+1}{x+1}$ is $0.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $q(x)={x}^{3}+kx+1.$ 

The remainder theorem states that when $q(x)$ is divided by $(x+1),$ the remainder equals $q(-1).$ Since we're told that the remainder is $0,$ then, we must have $q(-1)=0.$

Evaluating $q(-1)$ directly gives

$$
\begin{aligned}q(-1) & =(-1)^{3}+k(-1)+1 \\  & =-1-k+1 \\  & =-k,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that $k=0.$

$$

questions.problem: When $p(x)=9{x}^{3}+m{x}^{2}+x-2$ is divided by $3x-1$ the remainder is $2.$ What is the value of $m?$
questions.worked_solution:
The remainder theorem states that when $p(x)$ is divided by $3x-1=3(x-\frac{1}{3}),$ the remainder equals $p(\frac{1}{3}).$ Since we're told that the remainder is $2,$ then, we must have $p(\frac{1}{3})=2.$

Evaluating $p(\frac{1}{3})$ directly gives

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\frac{1}{3}) & =9{(\frac{1}{3})}^{3}+m{(\frac{1}{3})}^{2}+\frac{1}{3}-2 \\  & =\frac{1}{3}+\frac{m}{9}+\frac{1}{3}-2 \\  & =\frac{m}{9}-\frac{4}{3} \\  & =\frac{m-12}{9},\end{aligned}
$$

which means that

$$
2=\frac{m-12}{9}.
$$

Solving for $m$ in the equation above, we find that $m=30.$

questions.problem: Suppose $f(x)=a{x}^{2}+bx-6$ has a factor of $(x-3)$ and has a remainder of $-4$ when divided by $(x+1).$ Find the value of $a+b.$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $(x-3)$ is a factor of $f(x)$, it must divide into $f(x)$ with no remainder. In other words, when $f(x)$ is divided by $(x-3),$ the remainder is $0.$ It follows from the remainder theorem that

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =f(3) \\  & =a(3)^{2}+b(3)-6 \\  & =a(9)+b(3)-6 \\  & =9a+3b-6.\end{aligned}
$$

Likewise, since we're told that the remainder is $-4$ when $f(x)$ is divided by $(x+1),$ it follows from the remainder theorem that

$$
\begin{aligned}-4 & =f(-1) \\  & =a(-1)^{2}+b(-1)-6 \\  & =a(1)+b(-1)-6 \\  & =a-b-6.\end{aligned}
$$

We now have the system of equations

$$
\{\begin{aligned}0=9a+3b-6 \\ -4=a-b-6.\end{aligned}
$$

Simplifying each equation, we get

$$
\{\begin{aligned}3a+b=2 \\ a-b=2.\end{aligned}
$$

To eliminate $b,$ we add the equations and get

$$
\begin{aligned}3 & a+b &  & =2 \\ +\, & a-b &  & =2 \\ 4 & a &  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get $a=1.$ Finally, we substitute it into $a-b=2$ to find $b=-1.$ 

Therefore, our final solution is $(a,b)=(1,-1).$ 

Finally then, $a+b=1-1=0.$

questions.problem: Suppose $f(x)=a{x}^{2}+bx-10$ has a factor of $x+2$ and has a remainder of $18$ when divided by $x+4.$ Find the value of $a+b.$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $(x+2)$ is a factor of $f(x)$, it must divide into $f(x)$ with no remainder. In other words, when $f(x)$ is divided by $(x+2),$ the remainder is $0.$ It follows from the remainder theorem that

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =f(-2) \\  & =a(-2)^{2}+b(-2)-10 \\  & =a(4)+b(-2)-10 \\  & =4a-2b-10.\end{aligned}
$$

Likewise, since we're told that the remainder is $18$ when $f(x)$ is divided by $(x+4),$ it follows from the remainder theorem that

$$
\begin{aligned}18 & =f(-4) \\  & =a(-4)^{2}+b(-4)-10 \\  & =a(16)+b(-4)-10 \\  & =16a-4b-10.\end{aligned}
$$

We now have the system of equations

$$
\{\begin{aligned}0=4a-2b-10 \\ 18=16a-4b-10.\end{aligned}
$$

Simplifying each equation, we get

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2a-b=5 \\ 4a-b=7.\end{aligned}
$$

To eliminate $a,$ we subtract the equations and get

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & a-b &  & =7 \\ -\,2 & a-b &  & =5 \\ 2 & a &  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get $2a=2,$ and hence $a=1.$ Finally, we substitute it into $2a-b=5$ to find $b=-3.$ 

Therefore, our final solution is $(a,b)=(1,-3).$ 

Finally then, $a+b=1-3=-2$

canonical_examples.problem: Find the remainder when $p(x)=3x^2 +7x - 4$ is divided by $(3x-2).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The remainder theorem states that when $p(x)$ is divided by $(3x-2)= 3\left(x-\dfrac23\right),$ the remainder equals $p\left(\dfrac23\right).$ 

Evaluating $p\left(\dfrac23\right)$ directly gives

$$
\eqalign{
 		p\left(\dfrac23\right) & =3\cdot \left(\dfrac23\right)^2 +7\cdot \left(\dfrac23\right) - 4 \[5pt]
                        & =3\cdot \left(\dfrac49\right) +\dfrac{14}{3} - 4 \[5pt]
                        & =\dfrac{12}{9}+\dfrac{2}{3}  \[5pt]
 	                & = \dfrac{12+ 3\cdot 2}{9} \[5pt]
 			& = \dfrac{18}{9}\[5pt]
 			& = 2.
	}
$$

So, when $p(x)$ is divided by $3\left(x-\dfrac23\right),$ the remainder is $2.$

**Note:** We can check the answer by carrying out synthetic division:

|  | $x^2$ | $x^1$ | $x^0$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\color{red}\frac23$ | $3$ | $7$ | $\!\!\!\!-4$ |
|  | $\color{gray}\downarrow$ | $2$ | $6$ |
|  | $3$ | $9$ | $2$ |

canonical_examples.problem: If $q(x)=2x^3+3x^2-5x+c$ has remainder $-5$ when divided by $(x+3),$ what is the value of $c?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The remainder theorem states that when $q(x)$ is divided by $(x+3),$ the remainder equals $q(-3).$ Since we're told that the remainder is $-5,$ then, we must have $q(-3)=-5.$

Evaluating $q(-3)$ directly gives

$$
\begin{aligned}q(-3) & =2(-3)^{3}+3(-3)^{2}-5(-3)+c \\  & =-54+27+15+c \\  & =-12+c,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that

$$
-5 = -12 + c.
$$

Solving for $c$ in the equation above, we find that $c=7.$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding the Values of Two Unknowns in a Polynomial Given Two Remainders
canonical_examples.problem: Suppose $f(x) = ax^3 +bx^2 -11x -2$ has a factor of $(x-2)$ and remainder of $-8$ when divided by $(x-1).$ Find the values of $a$ and $b.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Since $(x-2)$ is a factor of $f(x)$, it must divide into $f(x)$ with no remainder. In other words, when $f(x)$ is divided by $(x-2),$ the remainder is $0.$ It follows from the remainder theorem that

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =f(2) \\  & =a(2)^{3}+b(2)^{2}-11(2)-2 \\  & =8a+4b-24.\end{aligned}
$$

Likewise, since we're told that the remainder is $-8$ when $f(x)$ is divided by $(x-1),$ it follows from the remainder theorem that

$$
\begin{aligned}-8 & =f(1) \\  & =a(1)^{3}+b(1)^{2}-11(1)-2 \\  & =a+b-13.\end{aligned}
$$

We now have the system of equations

$$
\{\begin{aligned}0=8a+4b-24 \\ -8=a+b-13.\end{aligned}
$$

Simplifying each equation, we get

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2a+b=6 \\ a+b=5.\end{aligned}
$$

To eliminate $b,$ we subtract the equations and get

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & a+b &  & =6 \\ -\, & a+b &  & =5 \\  & a &  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $a=1$ into $a+b=5$ to find $b=4.$ 

Therefore, our final solution is $(a,b) = (1,4).$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
The **remainder** theorem states that for any polynomial $p(x)$ and number $c,$ when we divide $p(x)$ by $(x-c),$ the remainder is equal to $p(c).$

For example, consider the polynomial $p(x)=4x^3-5x^2-7x+3$ and the number $c={\color{red}{2}}.$ First, let's divide $p(x)$ by $(x-{\color{red}{2}})$ using synthetic division:

|  | $x^3$ | $x^2$ | $x^1$ | $x^0$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\color{red}2$ | $4$ | $-5$ | $-7$ | $3$ |
|  | $\color{gray}\downarrow$ | $8$ | $6$ | $-2$ |
|  | $4$ | $3$ | $-1$ | $1$ |

We get a remainder of ${\color{blue}1}.$ Indeed, when we work out $p({\color{red}2}),$ we also get a result of ${\color{blue}1},$ just like the remainder theorem guarantees:

$$
\begin{aligned}p(2) & =4(2)^{3}-5(2)^{2}-7(2)+3 \\  & =32-20-14+3 \\  & =1\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

To understand why this happens, notice that we can use the result of the synthetic division to rewrite $p(x)$ as

$$
p(x) = (4x^2+3x-1)(x-2)+{\color{blue}{1}}.
$$

When we substitute $x={\color{red}{2}}$ into the above, we see that the $(x-2)$ factor turns to $0,$ thereby eliminating the quotient $(4x^2+3x-1)$ and leaving only the remainder of ${\color{blue}{1}}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}p(2) & =(4\cdot {2}^{2}+3\cdot 2-1)(2-2)+1 \\  & =(4\cdot {2}^{2}+3\cdot 2-1)(0)+1 \\  & =0+1 \\  & =1\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

The remainder theorem remains valid even if we substitute $(x-c)$ with $k(x-c),$ as long as $k$  is a non-zero real number. Let's look at an example.
